subject: Copywriting
title: Jingles: Songs That Sell
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Jingles: Songs That Sell.

hook.text: In 1926, the Wheaties jingle became the first radio ad song. Sales in Minneapolis jumped immediately.

buildup.text: Jingles exploited a quirk of memory: music sticks. You can't forget a tune even when you want to.

discovery.text: 'I'd like to buy the world a Coke' was so catchy it became a real pop song on the charts.

twist.text: By the 2000s, jingles fell out of fashion. Brands switched to licensed pop songs for credibility.

climax.text: 'Ba da ba ba ba, I'm lovin' it.' McDonald's proved jingles aren't dead—they just got shorter.

punchline.text: You're humming one right now. Jingles never left.

quiz.question: Which brand's jingle became an actual pop song?

details.summary: Advertising jingles — short, catchy songs written to sell products — dominated radio and TV advertising for decades. From 'I'd Like to Buy the World a Coke' to McDonald's 'I'm Lovin' It,' jingles use melody and repetition to embed brand messages in long-term memory more durably than spoken words...
details.whyItMatters: Music bypasses rational resistance and lodges directly in memory. Understanding why jingles work explains the power of sonic branding and audio marketing across all media.
takeaways: Jingles combine melody and repetition for superior memory encoding
Musical messages are stored differently and more durably than spoken ones
Sonic branding (audio logos, notification sounds) extends the jingle tradition

faq.question: Why are jingles so hard to forget?
faq.answer: Music is processed in a different brain region than speech. Melodies create 'earworms' — involuntary musical memories — that replay without conscious effort. Adding words to melody creates a dual-coded memory trace that is extraordinarily persistent.

faq.question: Are jingles still used in modern advertising?
faq.answer: Traditional jingles have declined, but sonic branding has grown. Netflix's 'ta-dum,' Apple's startup sound, and Intel's chime are modern jingles — brief sonic logos that trigger brand recognition. The principle is the same; the format has evolved.
